'''''Erodium''''' is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the botanical family [[Geraniaceae]]. The genus includes about 120 species with a subcosmopolitan distribution, [[native plant|native]] to Europe, [[North Africa]], [[Asia]], [[Australia]], and more locally in [[North America|North]] and [[South America]].<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |author-link1=Plants of the World Online |id=30013005-2 |title=''Erodium'' L'Hér. |access-date=22 June 2024 }}</ref> They are [[perennial]]s, [[annual plant|annual]]s, or [[subshrub]]s, with five-petalled flowers in shades of white, pink, and purple, that strongly resemble the better-known ''[[Geranium]]'' (crane's-bills).<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref> In English-speaking areas of Europe, the species are known as '''stork's-bills'''.<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020>{{cite web |title=Common Stork's-bill ''Erodium cicutarium'' agg. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.vff |access-date=22 June 2024 }}</ref> In North America they are known as '''filarees''' or '''heron's bill'''.{{citation needed|date=June 2024}}

== Taxonomy ==
[[Carl Linnaeus]] grouped in the same genus (''Geranium''), the three similar genera ''Erodium'', ''Geranium'', and ''[[Pelargonium]]''. The distinction between them was made by [[Charles Louis L'Héritier de Brutelle]] based on the number of [[stamen]]s or [[anther]]s; five in ''Erodium'',<ref name="Parnell">Parnell, J. and Curtis. ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref> seven for ''Pelargonium'', and ten for ''Geranium''.<ref name="Parnell"/> However, the three genera have the same characteristics in regard to their fruit, which resemble long bird beaks. That characteristic is the basis for the names: ''Geranium'' evokes the crane (Greek ''geranos''), ''Pelargonium'' the stork (''pelargos''), and ''Erodium'' the heron (''erodios''). ''Erodium'' species also differ in having [[pinnate]] leaves, whereas ''Geranium'' species have [[palmately]] lobed or divided leaves.<ref name = "Streeter">Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[File:Andre's Harvester Ant, Folsom, California, United States imported from iNaturalist photo 106809.jpg|thumb|''Erodium'' sp. seed carried by an [[Veromessor andrei|Andre's harvester ant]]]]
''Erodium'' species are used as food plants by the [[larva]]e of some [[Lepidoptera]] species including the [[pasture day moth]].

== Cultivation ==
In cultivation, ''Erodium'' species are usually seen in [[garden design#Rock garden|rockeries]] or [[alpine gardens]].<ref name=RHSAZ />

The [[Hybrid (biology)#Hybrid plants|hybrid]] [[cultivar]] ''E. × variabile'' 'Roseum' (''E. corsicum'' × ''E. reichardii''), a compact, spreading [[perennial plant|perennial]] with rose-pink flowers in summer, has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=''Erodium'' × ''variabile'' 'Roseum'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/81968/Erodium-x-variabile-Roseum/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=9 June 2020}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Species such as ''E. cicutarium'' and ''E. moschatum'' are edible.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nyerges |first1=Christopher |title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles |date=2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6 |page=81 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ}}</ref>
